query: For steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to corrosion? Specify a controlled study capable of revealing the governing cause, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting evidence from prior findings, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In high-Cr steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, severe plastic deformation that produces an ultrafine-grained microstructure will accelerate Cr diffusion to the surface, leading to the rapid formation of a continuous, Cr-enriched passivation film that significantly reduces corrosion rates compared to conventionally processed (coarse-grained) steels.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-Cr steel (e.g., similar to duplex stainless steel 2205) with standard, coarse-grained microstructure and typical alloying levels suitable for chemical and nuclear applications.
generation.intervention: Application of severe plastic deformation (e.g., high-pressure torsion or equivalent SPD technique) to reduce the grain size into the sub-micron (ultrafine-grained) regime.
generation.conditions: Corrosion tests conducted in simulated corrosive environments representative of chemical processing (e.g., acidic/neutral chloride solutions) and nuclear power (e.g., high-temperature water or relevant molten salt environments) under controlled temperature and pressure conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: A markedly increased grain-boundary area in the ultrafine-grained steel promotes enhanced Cr mobility and results in a more uniform, Cr-rich passivation film at the surface.
generation.mechanism: Severe plastic deformation induces nanostructuring that accelerates Cr diffusion along grain boundaries. This rapid diffusion leads to the preferential formation and stabilization of a protective, Cr-enriched passive film that resists further corrosive attack by acting as a physical and chemical barrier.
generation.predicted_outcome: Ultrafine-grained steel specimens will exhibit significantly lower corrosion current densities (expected reduction on the order of 30-50%) and slower weight loss rates with improved electrochemical parameters (e.g., more noble corrosion potentials) compared to coarse-grained control specimens.
generation.baseline: Coarse-grained high-Cr steel specimens processed by conventional methods, which form passivation films more slowly and exhibit higher corrosion rates under identical testing conditions.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold for steels containing adequate Cr (>10 wt%) under moderate to high temperature conditions (well below 650°C) in environments analogous to chemical processing and nuclear reactor service conditions. Extreme conditions (e.g., very high temperatures or highly oxidizing environments) may involve additional mechanisms.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative improvement in corrosion resistance may vary with the exact SPD process parameters, potential formation of undesirable secondary phases, and interaction with other alloying elements. Additionally, long-term stability of the ultrafine-grained structure under operational stress and irradiation is an open question.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-Cr steel specimens: one set processed via severe plastic deformation to obtain an ultrafine-grained structure and another set with conventional coarse-grained microstructure. Expose both sets to identical, controlled corrosive environments (e.g., 0.6 M NaCl solution at elevated temperatures typical of service conditions) and monitor corrosion behavior over a fixed duration.
measurements: Electrochemical measurements (potentiodynamic polarization to obtain corrosion current density and corrosion potential)
Surface chemical analysis (using XPS) to assess Cr enrichment in the passive film
Microstructural characterization (SEM/TEM) to verify grain size and film continuity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ultrafine-grained specimens do not show a statistically significant reduction (e.g., at least 30% lower corrosion current density and weight loss) compared to the coarse-grained controls, or if surface analysis fails to confirm enhanced Cr enrichment in the passive film, then the hypothesis that ultrafine-graining accelerates protective passivation film formation would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Development of materials suitable for molten fluoride salt environments started in the 1950s with the Aircraft Reactor Experiment (ARE). This experiment used Inconel 600 as a container material, however it was found that this material was not be suitable for high temperature molten fluoride salt applications. The Molten Salt Reactor Experiment (MSRE) at ORNL led to the development of Hastelloy N alloy as a structural material for fuel-bearing molten fluoride salt, which was demonstrated to have superior long-term corrosion resistance in molten fluoride salts. However, in fuel bearing molten salts, the fission product tellurium was noted to lead to crack formation in the alloy due to the precipitation of intermetallic compounds at the grain boundaries. In addition, in such high Ni-content alloys, additional embrittlement may be caused during irradiation. Transmutation of Ni can lead to the formation of helium that weaken the alloy grain boundaries. Several other traditional high temperature alloys have been tested in molten fluoride salts such as 316 L and 304 stainless steels, Incoloy 800 H, Inconel 617, Inconel 625, Hastelloy X, and Haynes 230.

Corrosion in molten salts is affected by several factors such as thermodynamics of corrosion reactions, elemental activities in the salt and the alloy, impurities, and temperature gradients. For instance, moisture in the salt can lead to the formation of hydrofluoric acid which can interact with metallic structural alloys and cause elemental dissolution into the salt. Also, metallic impurities incorporated in the salt may undergo exchange reactions to leach the least noble element out of the alloy. Most engineering alloys used in nuclear applications contain reasonable amounts of Cr to provide protection against air oxidation, and typically, chromium is the most vulnerable alloying element to fluoride salt corrosion.

As a well-known high-entropy alloys (HEA), equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi alloy, also known as Cantor alloy, has been increasingly investigated in recent years, with a focus on enhanced fracture toughness and ductility at cryogenic temperatures []. HEAs could become future materials for structural applications due to these superior properties. However, compared with the mechanical properties, the corrosion properties, which are also important for structural applications, have not been investigated to the same extent. The majority of HEAs, as represented by Cantor alloy, have a higher amount of Cr and Ni compared to commercial stainless steels (SS) such as AISI304, so that they are expected to exhibit high corrosion resistance, and they have been demonstrated to possess high passivating capability in neutral solutions [,,,,,]. However, it seems that the corrosion resistance of HEAs is not necessarily as high as expected given the large Cr and Ni content [,,], and in particular the pitting corrosion resistance in chloride-containing environments is inferior to AISI304 [,,]. Severe plastic deformation (SPD) techniques enable the fabrication of ultrafine-grained (UFG) or nanocrystalline (NC) materials in bulk forms suitable for load-carrying structural applications []. With the advent of SPD, there has been an increasing demand to clarify the effect of UFG/NC formation on corrosion from a practical viewpoint, especially with regard to the classic topic of the effect of grain size on corrosion [,]. Among the various materials investigated to date, stainless steels exhibited mostly improved corrosion resistance by forming UFG structures by SPD [,,,,,,,]. The enhanced corrosion resistance of UFG/NC SSs compared with coarse-grained (CG) materials has been mostly attributed to greater Cr enrichment in the passivation film [,,,,,,,,], which has been validated experimentally by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) [] and recently by Cs-corrected scanning-transmission electron microscopy (STEM) [,]. Two possibilities for the enhanced Cr enrichment in the passivation film of UFG/NC materials have been proposed. Dual-phase high entropy alloys have recently attracted widespread attention as advanced structural materials due to their unique microstructure, excellent mechanical properties, and corrosion resistance. However, their molten salt corrosion behavior has not been reported, which is critical in evaluating their application merit in the areas of concentrating solar power and nuclear energy. Here, the molten salt corrosion behavior of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was evaluated in molten NaCl-KCl-MgCl2 salt at 450 °C and 650 °C in comparison to conventional duplex stainless steel 2205 (DS2205). The EHEA showed a significantly lower corrosion rate of ~1 mm/year at 450 °C compared to ~8 mm/year for DS2205. Similarly, EHEA showed a lower corrosion rate of ~9 mm/year at 650 °C compared to ~20 mm/year for DS2205. There was selective dissolution of the body-centered cubic phase in both the alloys, B2 in AlCoCrFeNi2.1 and α-Ferrite in DS2205. This was attributed to micro-galvanic coupling between the two phases in each alloy that was measured in terms of Volta potential difference using a scanning kelvin probe. papers.title: Molten Salt Corrosion Behavior of Dual-Phase High Entropy Alloy for Concentrating Solar Power Systems.
papers.system: Dual-phase alloys compared with duplex steel 2205 (a benchmark steel used in high-temperature corrosive environments)
papers.approach: Exposed samples to molten NaCl–KCl–MgCl2 salt at 450 °C and 650 °C; measured corrosion rates and used scanning Kelvin probe analysis to assess local electrochemical activity.
papers.findings: DS2205 exhibited corrosion rates around ~8 mm/year at 450 °C and ~20 mm/year at 650 °C, while the novel HEA performed significantly better. The study highlighted selective dissolution of one phase driven by micro-galvanic coupling.
papers.mechanism: Micro-galvanic coupling between the two phases in dual-phase steels leads to selective attack; the protective role of a secondary phase (e.g., an FCC-like phase) may retard oxidation if enriched in noble elements.

papers.title: Corrosion and Thermal Stability of CrMnFeNi High Entropy Alloy in Molten FLiBe Salt.
papers.system: High-entropy alloy in a molten fluoride salt environment; discussion provided context with conventional nuclear alloys (e.g., 316L stainless steel, Inconel series) used in nuclear reactors.
papers.approach: Examined corrosion behavior in molten FLiBe salt at high temperatures, with attention paid to key alloying elements (notably chromium) and the impacts of impurities (e.g., moisture leading to HF formation).
papers.findings: Chromium, while crucial for passivation in many steels, is the most vulnerable element in fluoride salt environments due to its tendency to dissolve. Precipitation of Cr-rich phases may be beneficial if they enhance the formation of a stable passivation layer.
papers.mechanism: Corrosion is governed by thermodynamic factors, elemental activities, and the selective dissolution of Cr due to micro-galvanic effects between phases. This suggests that the protective passivation may fail if Cr is depleted.

papers.title: Corrosion Behavior of Ultrafine-Grained CoCrFeMnNi High-Entropy Alloys Fabricated by High-Pressure Torsion.
papers.system: Ultrafine-grained (UFG) stainless steels (using a high-entropy alloy analogue with high Cr and Ni contents) compared with their coarse-grained counterparts.
papers.approach: Utilized severe plastic deformation (via high-pressure torsion) to produce nanocrystalline structures and evaluated corrosion in acid and chloride environments.
papers.findings: The UFG materials exhibited enhanced corrosion resistance compared to coarse-grained versions. This enhancement was attributed to the formation of a passivation film with enriched Cr content (confirmed by techniques such as XPS and STEM).
papers.mechanism: Refinement of grain structure increases the grain boundary area, thereby accelerating Cr diffusion and promoting rapid formation of a protective passivation film that resists localized attack.

established: High-Cr content in steels is a key factor in developing a stable passivation film that imparts corrosion resistance.
Dual-phase steels and nanostructured stainless steels can harness microstructural features (phase distribution, grain boundaries) to control corrosion behavior.
Corrosion in high-temperature and aggressive chemical environments (molten salts, nuclear reactor coolants) is strongly influenced by elemental segregation and micro-galvanic effects.

approaches_tried.approach: Employing severe plastic deformation (e.g., high-pressure torsion) to produce ultrafine-grained steels that enhance Cr segregation in passivation films.
approaches_tried.outcome: Improved corrosion resistance due to more rapid and uniform formation of protective layers; record_ids: ["PMC8838792::web::003::1_introduction", "PMC8838792::web::001::1_introduction"]

approaches_tried.approach: Comparative evaluation of dual-phase steels versus novel alloy systems in molten salt environments.
approaches_tried.outcome: Revealed that although micro-galvanic coupling can lead to local selective dissolution, correct phase balance (or engineered protective phases) can yield lower overall corrosion rates; record_ids: ["PMC9955357::web::003::1_introduction"]

mechanisms: Formation of a Cr-rich passivation film via diffusion along grain boundaries.
Micro-galvanic coupling between distinct phases leading to selective dissolution and localized corrosion.
Thermodynamic and kinetic factors governing the dissolution of vulnerable species (notably Cr) in aggressive environments.
disagreements: Some studies indicate that high Cr and Ni contents do not always guarantee high corrosion resistance in all environments (e.g., pitting in chloride solutions), suggesting that microstructure and phase distribution play critical roles.
There is debate over whether the observed enhanced corrosion resistance in ultrafine-grained steels is solely due to Cr enrichment or if other defect-related mechanisms also contribute significantly.
open_questions: How do specific microstructural features (grain size, phase boundaries, and local chemical ordering) quantitatively control the initiation and propagation of corrosion in steels under chemical processing and nuclear reactor conditions?

What is the interplay between micro-galvanic effects and passivation film stability in complex multi-phase steels, particularly under long-term exposure to molten salt or high-temperature aqueous environments?
How do irradiation and high-temperature aging impact the mechanisms of Cr diffusion and passivation film formation in steels?
opportunities: Design controlled studies that vary grain size, phase fraction, and local chemical order in steels to isolate the effect of each variable on passivation film formation and stability.
Apply in situ techniques (e.g., scanning Kelvin probe, XPS) during corrosion tests in simulated nuclear and chemical processing environments to track dynamic changes in the protective film.

Combine advanced microstructural characterization with accelerated corrosion testing to determine the boundaries (temperature, chemical composition, irradiation dose) within which the Cr-driven passivation mechanism remains effective.

directions.direction: Composition design: Increase Cr (and possibly Ni) content to optimize the formation of a protective passivation film on steels.
directions.assessment: This direction directly targets the corrosion resistance by ensuring enough Cr is available for passivation. It is well supported by evidence describing the role of Cr in resisting corrosion (e.g., PMC6908586::web::009::corrosion_behavior) and by studies on conventional stainless steel. However, adding more Cr alone may meet processing or cost constraints and may not address the influence of microstructural features.

directions.direction: Processing route via severe plastic deformation (SPD) to produce ultrafine-grained steels that promote rapid Cr diffusion and enriched passivation film development.
directions.assessment: This option directly addresses the limitation of passivation film kinetics. By refining grain size, excessive grain-boundary density expedites Cr migration to the surface, forming a uniform, dense passive layer. Evidence from ultrafine-grained stainless steels (PMC8838792::web::003::1_introduction, PMC8838792::web::001::1_introduction) supports this mechanism. It respects the application conditions for chemical processing and nuclear power and is a feasible, informative study.

directions.direction: Tailored dual-phase steel microstructures to control micro-galvanic coupling between phases, thereby minimizing localized corrosion.
directions.assessment: This strategy exploits phase distribution to balance galvanic effects, as suggested by studies on dual-phase alloys (PMC9955357::web::003::1_introduction). Although promising, controlling phase fractions with high precision under industrial conditions may be challenging and the mechanistic signature is less directly linked to passivation film formation.

directions.direction: Surface engineering via applying nanostructured coatings that mimic native passivation layers (e.g., doping with noble elements)
directions.assessment: While this approach may provide excellent corrosion resistance, it represents an additive solution rather than explaining inherent material resistance mechanisms. It may also not fully satisfy constraints for steels in high-temperature or irradiation environments typical of nuclear power.

directions.direction: In-situ advanced characterization of passivation film evolution (e.g., using scanning Kelvin probe or XPS) under simulated operational environments.
directions.assessment: This direction can reveal the interfacial kinetics and local chemical changes governing corrosion resistance. It is highly informative to validate mechanisms but is more of an observational study rather than an intervention that directly improves resistance. The study’s sophistication may limit its immediate applicability for engineering design.

choice.direction: Processing route via severe plastic deformation (SPD) to produce ultrafine-grained steels that promote rapid Cr diffusion and enriched passivation film development.
choice.why: This direction directly tests the mechanistic hypothesis that a refined microstructure accelerates Cr diffusion along a high density of grain boundaries, forming a more protective, uniformly enriched passivation film. It leverages known physics and previous observations (e.g., enhanced corrosion resistance in ultrafine-grained steels as reported in PMC8838792::web::003::1_introduction and PMC8838792::web::001::1_introduction) while remaining feasible in controlled laboratory environments relevant to chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications.
